candidateArtifact.completeText:
# LUMINAiRY profile candidate

Name: Hannah Fry
Role: Keeper of the Explanation

About: Fry makes the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question. The 2026 Leelavati Prize recognized her contribution to increasing public awareness of mathematics. In Hello World, she asks who should decide a criminal case—a person or an algorithm—and who should decide who receives a life-saving liver. Penguin describes the book as examining algorithms' power, limitations and whether they improve on human decisions. LAiDIES calls her Keeper of the Explanation because she turns a hidden system into questions a reader can use: What is it trying to achieve? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence?

Lesson: Make an invisible technical system understandable by showing where it touches ordinary decisions.

Image: /assets/mavens/y2k-stained-glass-v4-dark-sapphire/hannah-fry-y2k-stained-glass.png

Resources (preserved exactly):
- read: Read Cambridge profile — https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/person/hf418
- watch: Watch AI Confidential — https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/m002q76d/ai-confidential-with-hannah-fry-series-1-1-the-boy-who-tried-to-kill-the-queen
- listen: Listen to The Rest Is Science — https://therestis.com/science
- listen: Listen to Google DeepMind: The Podcast — https://deepmind.google/the-podcast/
- watch: Watch Hannah Fry on YouTube — https://www.youtube.com/@fryrsquared
- follow: Follow Hannah Fry on Instagram — https://www.instagram.com/fryrsquared/
- follow: Follow Hannah Fry on X — https://x.com/FryRsquared

Freshness: Role and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026

reverseBrief.humanQuestion: Why does LAiDIES celebrate Hannah Fry — what does she actually do for a beginner reader, beyond holding an impressive title?
reverseBrief.promisedPayoff: A reader finishes the card knowing what Fry contributes (making the math inside automated decisions questionable by ordinary people), one vivid example of it, and a set of portable questions she can use herself.
reverseBrief.distinctiveContribution: Fry makes the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question, recognized by the 2026 Leelavati Prize for increasing public awareness of mathematics.
reverseBrief.concreteExample: Hello World's paired dilemmas: who should decide a criminal case — a person or an algorithm — and who should decide who receives a life-saving liver.
reverseBrief.readerConsequence: The reader gains three usable questions to aim at any hidden system: What is it trying to achieve? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence?
reverseBrief.usefulEntryPoint: Hello World as the named starting text, backed by seven preserved read/watch/listen/follow links (Cambridge profile, AI Confidential, two podcasts, YouTube, Instagram, X).

incumbentControl.reason: The incumbent About ('Cambridge lists Fry as Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics.') is title-only biography. It supplies no distinctive contribution, no concrete example, no reader consequence and no entry point — it fails the reader job on every earned dimension, independently of the candidate's outcome.

plainClarity.reason: Every sentence is plain, third-person and jargon-free; 'automated decisions', 'algorithm' and 'hidden system' are the hardest terms and each is grounded in an everyday situation (criminal case, liver transplant). 99 words fits a shared card.
plainClarity.artifactExcerpt: Fry makes the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question.

distinctiveContribution.reason: The card names what Fry does (makes hidden math questionable by ordinary people) rather than merely what she is; the Leelavati recognition is used as evidence for that contribution, not as award-list substitution — only one honour is cited, in service of the claim.
distinctiveContribution.artifactExcerpt: The 2026 Leelavati Prize recognized her contribution to increasing public awareness of mathematics.

concreteExample.reason: Two specific, consequential dilemmas from Hello World make the abstract contribution tangible, and both map directly to the publisher's own framing questions.
concreteExample.artifactExcerpt: she asks who should decide a criminal case—a person or an algorithm—and who should decide who receives a life-saving liver

readerConsequence.reason: The About hands the reader a portable capability, not just admiration: three questions she can aim at any automated system in her own life. The lesson line reinforces it.
readerConsequence.artifactExcerpt: questions a reader can use: What is it trying to achieve? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence?

usefulEntryPoint.reason: Hello World is named and characterized so a beginner knows why to open it, and the seven preserved links give tiered entry (read, watch, listen, follow) without link confetti in the prose itself.
usefulEntryPoint.artifactExcerpt: Penguin describes the book as examining algorithms' power, limitations and whether they improve on human decisions.

surfaceFit.reason: About is 99 words in a single coherent paragraph; role, lesson, image, freshness and all seven links are present in card format with no overflow, headers, or scaffolding inside the About field.
surfaceFit.artifactExcerpt: Lesson: Make an invisible technical system understandable by showing where it touches ordinary decisions.

voice.reason: Warm, factual, third-person editorial voice; attribution is honest ('Penguin describes', 'LAiDIES calls her'); no first-person founder voice, no template repetition, no generic inspirational closer — it ends on the three working questions.
voice.artifactExcerpt: LAiDIES calls her Keeper of the Explanation because she turns a hidden system into questions a reader can use

lockedFieldPreservation.reason: The artifact text matches the successor profile exactly on role, lesson, image, all seven links (order, labels, URLs) and freshness; only About differs from the incumbent, consistent with the change proof's byte-identical link claim.
lockedFieldPreservation.artifactExcerpt: Freshness: Role and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026

facts.reason: Cambridge (primary institution) states the prize and its rationale; the candidate's paraphrase 'increasing public awareness of mathematics' matches the citation, and the 2026 dating matches the ICM 2026 announcement context on the same page.
facts.artifactExcerpt: The 2026 Leelavati Prize recognized her contribution to increasing public awareness of mathematics.
facts.sourceExcerpt: awarded the Leelavati Prize at the International Congress of Mathematicians for outstanding contributions to increasing the public awareness of mathematics

facts.reason: Both dilemmas are drawn directly from Penguin's book description; 'who should decide a criminal case' is a fair compression of 'who would you rather determined your fate' for an accused person, and the liver-allocation question is near-verbatim. Publisher-copy limit respected: the card reports the book's questions, not their answers.
facts.artifactExcerpt: she asks who should decide a criminal case—a person or an algorithm—and who should decide who receives a life-saving liver
facts.sourceExcerpt: You are accused of a crime. Who would you rather determined your fate – a human or an algorithm? ... You need a liver transplant to save your life. Who would you want in charge of organ allocation?

facts.reason: The candidate explicitly attributes this to Penguin and stays inside the publisher's own words (power, limitations, improvement on humans), correctly avoiding the unsourced promotional claim that algorithms are 'less prone to error'.
facts.artifactExcerpt: Penguin describes the book as examining algorithms' power, limitations and whether they improve on human decisions.
facts.sourceExcerpt: demonstrates their power, exposes their limitations, and examines whether they really are an improvement on the humans they are replacing

facts.reason: The lead sentence is an editorial synthesis, not a verbatim source claim. It is reasonably grounded in the Leelavati citation about translating mathematics for the public and in Hello World's scope (algorithms making important decisions), but 'automated decisions' narrows the sourced 'mathematics' framing; acceptable as interpretive framing given the two anchors that follow.
facts.artifactExcerpt: Fry makes the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question.
facts.sourceExcerpt: she has used outstanding creativity and originality to translate mathematics into a language of wonder and relevance for the public

facts.reason: The 'Keeper of the Explanation' naming is explicitly attributed to LAiDIES as internal editorial framing and matches the locked role field exactly; it makes no external factual assertion requiring outside sourcing.
facts.artifactExcerpt: LAiDIES calls her Keeper of the Explanation because she turns a hidden system into questions a reader can use
facts.sourceExcerpt: Hannah Fry is one of the foremost global ambassadors for mathematical thinking

transfer.scenario: A reader learns her health insurer now uses an automated system to review physiotherapy claims, and her claim for her father's Tuesday sessions comes back reduced with no explanation.
transfer.question: Do the card's closing questions give her a usable way in, without requiring any technical knowledge or any assumed facts about the insurer's system?
transfer.answer: Yes. She can ask the insurer: What is this system trying to achieve — cost control, fraud detection, or clinical appropriateness? What might it miss — could it fail to see the referral letter or the treatment history that a human reviewer would weigh? Who carries the consequence if it is wrong — me, and what appeal route exists to a person? Each question is a request for information or a possibility to check, not an assertion about how the system actually works.
transfer.assessment: The three questions transfer cleanly to a new consequential automated decision. They generate concrete inquiries and possibilities without inventing the unseen system's objective, inputs or causal behavior as fact. The transfer test passes.

issues.finding: 'Who should decide a criminal case' slightly compresses Penguin's framing ('who would you rather determined your fate' when 'accused of a crime'), which is about sentencing/fate rather than deciding the whole case. The meaning survives for a beginner reader, but a stricter paraphrase would be 'who should decide your fate in a criminal case'. Not verdict-affecting.
issues.artifactExcerpt: she asks who should decide a criminal case—a person or an algorithm

issues.finding: The opening synthesis sentence narrows the sourced recognition (public awareness of mathematics broadly) to 'automated decisions' specifically. It is defensible because the Hello World anchor immediately substantiates the automated-decisions focus, but the lead claim itself rests on inference across two sources rather than a single passage.
issues.artifactExcerpt: Fry makes the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question.

learningDisposition.rationale: The candidate passes with only minor paraphrase-tightness observations; the only REJECT-level pattern encountered (title-only biography with no contribution, example, consequence or entry point) is the already-documented incumbent defect that motivated this replacement, confirmed by the negative control. No new reusable defect family emerged.

judgment.summary: PASS. The candidate About earns the celebration in 99 words: a distinctive contribution (making the math inside automated decisions questionable by ordinary people), a concrete sourced example (Hello World's criminal-case and liver-allocation dilemmas), a real reader consequence (three portable questions), and a clear entry point (Hello World plus seven preserved links). Every factual claim maps to Cambridge primary or explicitly-attributed Penguin publisher copy, with the publisher limit respected — the card avoids Penguin's unsupported 'less prone to error' promotion. All locked fields (role, lesson, image, seven byte-identical links, freshness) are preserved. The closing questions transfer to an unseen automated decision (insurance claim review) as genuine questions, not asserted facts. Two minor, non-material issues: a slight compression of Penguin's criminal-fate framing, and a lead sentence that is cross-source synthesis rather than single-passage fact. The incumbent negative control independently earns REJECT as title-only biography.

limitations: AI editorial assessment; no observed human comprehension is claimed.
Penguin is publisher copy. It supports the book example and scope, not independent evaluation.
This review does not sign, integrate or publish the profile.
